doc.title: Jimmy Wormworth interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 6, 2002

title: Nat Cole, Art Tatum and Nellie Lutcher records as a child
summary: A 1946 family record purchase starts his obsession with Nat Cole, Tatum and Lutcher.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Well you ended up playing with one of your childhood heroes, or heroines should I say—

Uh, in 1946 around January, not long after Christmas, one of my uncles who was stationed in the Pacific in World War II came home and with some of the money he had saved from his allotment, which he sent to my grandmother, not long after he got home he was influenced by probably my Uncle Dick and maybe my aunts, to buy a record player, well what in those days was called a combination. It’s a console record player and radio, when there was still 78s. It was the latest thing. Zenith. And so he bought this record player and radio combination and I can remember on the weekend, probably around March of ’46, which was maybe two or three months after my uncle was discharged from the service and came home, my mother and one or two of my aunts and my Uncle Dick and my Uncle Alfred went to the Melody House record store, which used to be on Blandina Street, just off Genesee Street, just east of Genesee Street, and they were having this huge sale on records. And the records were all 78s then. And I can remember going there with them and they just bought up all kinds of records. And the records ranged from Tommy Dorsey’s band with one or two records where Buddy Rich played solos, to I guess Tommy Dorsey’s band with Jo Stafford and all kinds of records, including Nellie Lutcher’s latest hits, an album on Capitol-Americana of Art Tatum and a whole bunch of Nat Cole trio singles. And I think that’s really when my obsession or my interest in playing really took off. I think I was nine or ten. And I just gravitated toward these Nat Cole trio records and Nellie Lutcher’s trio records, which were big hits. Nat Cole was pretty popular but that was before he became just a singer and stopped playing. But it was after he was just a pianist and played with Jazz at the Philharmonic and made records with whoever. He was a great pianist, I think that’s pretty indisputable. I think

that’s why he was such a good singer. He had a good instrument, good vocal chords and such knowledge. So those records and those Art Tatum records just took me off in the whole direction of music. I used to beg — I was spoiled rotten — and I’d beg my mother and my aunts, “Oh I don’t feel good, could I stay home from school?” “All right honey, what’s wrong?” And I’d stay home and all I would do is play those records over and over, and play passages. I got to the point when I was about 11 where I had a lot of the passages memorized, Art Tatum passages and whole Nat Cole records, each record memorized, the solos, the vocals, the intro, the endings.
